l: FlashRAG, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: FlashRAG is a modular, efficient open-source research toolkit for retrieval-augmented generation experiments, developed concurrently with a unified framework. It introduces similar work but lacks in-depth analysis of retrieval-related components.

l: experimental setups, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Experimental setups in RAG studies are fragmented across datasets, collections, metrics, retrieval systems, and LLMs, preventing systematic comparison of methods and pipeline components.

l: RAG evaluation, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: does_not_allow systematic comparison [across methods or components in the pipeline] RAG evaluation is presented as chaotic because studies use inconsistent datasets, collections, metrics, retrieval systems, LLMs, and data-processing choices. The unit argues that standardized evaluation is needed to compare RAG methods and components systematically.

l: retrieval, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: The impact of retrieval quality and its relative impact compared with LLM size remain unclear. The unit states that retrieval's contribution to improving responses is underexplored.

l: retrieval quality, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Retrieval quality is an important but insufficiently analyzed factor in RAG, significantly affecting response generation. It is linked to ranking, while many approaches use outdated retrievers without ranking refinement. Fine-tuning ranking models on target collections and using state-of-the-art rerankers improve ranking quality and context relevance; its impact relative to language model size remains unclear.

l: re-ranking, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Re-ranking is an often-overlooked critical aspect of retrieval quality. After an initial retrieval system, it adds a DeBERTa-v3 ranking stage. It is evaluated in comparisons of retrieval and generation quality, closes gaps between approaches, improves BM25, RetroMAE, and SPLADE-v3 results, but can hurt E5 retrieval effectiveness on NQ.

l: large language models, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Large language models are a language model class evaluated mainly zero-shot in RAG experiments because fine-tuning state-of-the-art models is computationally demanding. They receive top-5 passages and can benefit from improved retrieval methods at any size; model size does not generally predict retrieval benefit, though fine-tuning benefits smaller models more. They are discussed across retrieval, instruction following, hallucination, tool use, embeddings, evaluation, and model families.

l: data processing, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Data processing varies through preprocessing and Wikipedia snapshot choices, complicating comparisons and affecting observed performance.

l: datasets, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Datasets are supported in limited selections by LlamaIndex, DSPy, and RAGGED; differing evaluation choices fragment experiments and hinder comparison. BERGEN uses a computationally limited set and plans broader, multilingual evaluation.

l: ranking system R, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: R is a multi-staged ranking system that builds search index I from a collection, then searches it at request time to produce context segments relevant to user input x.

l: search index I, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Search index I is built from a collection, then searched at request time to yield context segments relevant to input.

l: context segments c, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Context segments are retrieved from an index by ranking systems using user input, chiefly as passages, and supplied through different retrieval systems to evaluate LLMs.

l: user input x, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: The user input x is used by the ranking system to retrieve relevant context segments c. It is also provided to the language model along with c to generate r.

l: response r, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Response r is generated by parametric generative language model θ from user input x and context segments c embedded in instruction template i.

l: model-specific instruction template i, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Model-specific template embeds user input and context segments, yielding instruction for the parametric generative language model to generate r.

l: Hugging Face Hub, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: The Hugging Face Hub provides the model and dataset infrastructure on which BERGEN is built. BERGEN uses it to access hosted or locally stored resources and to make adding further models and datasets straightforward.

l: Pyserini, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: is_a Python toolkit [for reproducible information retrieval research] It is described as a Python toolkit for reproducible information retrieval research using sparse and dense representations.

l: RetroMAE, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: RetroMAE is a dense retriever trained for MS MARCO passage ranking; its reranked version generally improves zero-shot generation and retrieval, with varying performance.

l: BGE-M3, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: BGE-M3 is a publicly available multilingual retriever supporting monolingual and cross-lingual retrieval; trained on considered languages, it effectively retrieves from concatenated multilingual Wikipedia and dynamically selects an appropriate datastore.

l: SOLAR-10.7B-Instruct-v1.0, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: is_a model SOLAR-10.7B-Instruct-v1.0 is used to judge whether an AI-generated answer is correct according to a question and golden answer.

l: MKQA, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: MKQA is a linguistically diverse, parallel multilingual open-domain question answering benchmark containing 10,000 Natural Questions examples translated into 25 languages, grounded primarily in English Wikipedia; experiments use a 2.7k-sample KILT NQ-overlapping subset and favor English Wikipedia retrieval.

l: XOR-TyDi QA, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: A multilingual question-answering dataset with 40,000 information-seeking questions in seven languages, grounded in same-language or English Wikipedia; 3,000 validation questions show multilingual retrieval outperforms English-only retrieval.

l: KILT, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: KILT is a benchmark for knowledge-intensive language tasks. It contains a fixed publicly available Wikipedia dump and passage- and document-level annotations of gold documents containing answers. Its datasets include ranking labels and are used to evaluate retrieval quality and effectiveness, compare retrieval with downstream generation, and support experiments on oracle passages and multilingual RAG.

l: Match, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Match is a non-commercial evaluation metric that measures exact label containment in generated answers and ranks among the most effective metrics tested.

l: Recall, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: is_a non-commercial metric [effective for zero-shot RAG evaluation] Recall compares the generated answer and label at the token level. It is identified as one of the most effective non-commercial metrics for zero-shot RAG evaluation, after LLMeval and alongside Match.

l: GPT-4, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: is_a large language model [technical report subject] It is covered by a technical report from OpenAI and colleagues.

l: RAGAS, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: is_a automated evaluation method [for retrieval augmented generation] It is presented as an automated evaluation method for retrieval-augmented generation.

l: QLoRA, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: is_a fine-tuning method [efficient and quantized] QLoRa is used to fine-tune the LLMs on NQ with SPLADE-v3 retrieval and DeBERTa-v3 reranking. Fine-tuning benefits smaller LLMs more and substantially reduces the performance gap between the 1.1B and 70B models.

l: answer equivalence evaluation, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Answer equivalence evaluation in BERGEN compares a generated response with a reference answer to determine whether the question has been answered sufficiently. The library supports both surface-based metrics and semantic or LLM-based approaches, including LLMeval, BEM, and GPT-4.

l: open-ended text generation evaluation, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: The experiments compare surface-based and LLM-based metrics for evaluating open-ended text generation. Longer answer-reference pairs are especially difficult for surface metrics and BEM.

l: GPT-4-as-a-judge, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: is_a strong evaluation baseline GPT-4-as-a-judge is used as the reference for comparing evaluation metrics. LLMeval most closely aligns with its judgments on average.

l: SOLAR-10.7B, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: SOLAR-10.7B serves as an answer generator with SPLADE-v3 retrieval; higher retrieval quality improves downstream RAG, and oracle retrieval beats closed-book generation though its gain is not largest.

l: TinyLlama-1.1B, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: gains_from fine-tuning [more than bigger counterparts on NQ] TinyLlama-1.1B is evaluated with and without oracle retrieval and gains from retrieval. After QLoRa fine-tuning on NQ, it reaches 0.77 LLMeval, a gain of 0.41 over its zero-shot result, which is the largest reported fine-tuning gain.

l: Llama2-7B, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: outperforms Llama2-70B [with retrieval versus without retrieval] Llama2-7B gains the most from oracle retrieval among the evaluated models. Its retrieved performance exceeds that of Llama2-70B without retrieval, and fine-tuning raises its LLMeval to 0.82, a gain of 0.24.

l: Llama2-70B, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Llama2-70B is evaluated for model-size effects and benefits from oracle retrieval, though less than Llama2-7B. Fine-tuning raises its LLMeval to 0.85, a gain of 0.06.

l: Llama3-8B, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Llama3-8B is included in comparisons of retrieval gains across LLM sizes. Fine-tuning raises its LLMeval to 0.78, a gain of 0.04 over zero-shot performance.

l: Command-R-35B, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Command-R-35B is a multilingual generator developed for RAG applications, officially supporting 11 languages; used in BERGEN experiments, it includes Russian only in pretraining and may answer English-context prompts in English.

l: MTEB, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: MTEB is the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark. It provides models examined in retrieval analysis, including models fine-tuned on NQ; its SoTA models achieve better retrieval and generation performance.

s: are_crucial evaluation [in addition to commonly used surface-matching metrics] Semantic evaluations are identified as crucial in addition to commonly used surface-matching metrics. They are recommended for evaluating RAG systems.

l: RAG response generation, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: RAG response generation is significantly affected by retrieval quality. This finding underscores the importance of strong retrieval methods in RAG systems.

l: knowledge-intensive tasks, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation

l: retrieval methods, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation

l: Unsupervised Information Refinement Training of Large Language Models for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: This is a paper in the Proceedings of the 62nd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, titled “Unsupervised Information Refinement Training of Large Language Models for Retrieval-Augmented Generation,” by Shicheng Xu, Liang Pang, Mo Yu, Fandong Meng, Huawei Shen, Xueqi Cheng, and Jie Zhou. It addresses a central weakness of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): large language models can be misled or hindered by retrieved text that is noisy, incomplete, incorrect, or lacks a direct answer. The authors propose treating the model as an “Information Refiner” that combines retrieved knowledge with its parameterized knowledge to generate concise, accurate, and complete responses. The paper introduces INFO-RAG, an unsupervised, low-cost, task-general training method. It frames retrieval through three scenarios: texts that contain all needed knowledge; texts with incomplete or incorrect knowledge; and semantically relevant texts without a usable answer. Correspondingly, INFO-RAG trains models on Select and Copy, Correct and Complete, and Contextual Stimulation tasks. Training data are built from English Wikipedia using sentence prefixes, target continuations, and simulated retrieved texts; pretrained models learn through prefix language modeling and next-token prediction. The three tasks are mixed with LoRA training in proportions of 20%, 40%, and 40%. Experiments span 11 datasets and seven task types, including question answering, slot filling, multi-hop and long-form question answering, dialogue, language modeling, and code generation. Across LLaMA-2-7B, LLaMA-2-7B-chat, LLaMA-2-13B, and LLaMA-2-13B-chat, INFO-RAG improves zero-shot RAG performance by an average of 9.39% in reported results. It also improves in-context learning, robustness to changes in retrieval results, and SearChain in open retrieval. Analysis finds that Correct and Complete and Contextual Stimulation are especially beneficial, while Select and Copy is most useful in combination with them; added Wikipedia training alone does not improve the backbone. INFO-RAG also avoids substantial catastrophic forgetting on MMLU without RAG. The paper concludes that unsupervised information-refinement training can help RAG models use retrieval more effectively. Its main limitation is evaluation only at 7B and 13B parameter sizes because of computing constraints. The authors state compliance with the ACL Ethics Policy and acknowledge support from several Chinese research programs and organizations.

l: Large Language Models, Unsupervised Information Refinement Training of Large Language Models for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Large Language Models are current mainstream decoder-only models used in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to provide additional knowledge and mitigate hallucination. They are pre-trained before RAG use, but that training does not clearly teach them to use retrieved texts of varied quality as references. Consequently, they can ignore or be misled by incorrect or noisy information, struggle to extract correct answers from long, complex texts, and fail to integrate their parameter knowledge when retrieved texts cannot address a task. The work proposes continuing unsupervised training so they become Information Refiners. In this role, they refine information through next-token prediction, learn from prefixes and retrieved texts, and use layer-wise word distributions to identify informative tokens. They are trained to extract relevant knowledge, remove irrelevant material, verify and rectify incorrect retrieved knowledge, complete missing knowledge, and use semantically relevant context to stimulate knowledge within their parameters. Across the scenarios, they verify, correct, and complete retrieved knowledge, then combine retrieved texts with knowledge in their parameters to solve questions. The intended result is an LLM that integrates both knowledge sources and generates text that is more concise, accurate, and complete regardless of retrieved texts' correctness, completeness, or usefulness.

l: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Unsupervised Information Refinement Training of Large Language Models for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Retrieval-Augmented Generation is a framework for modern NLP systems that enhances large language models by incorporating information retrieved from external databases or texts as context for generation. It supports text-generation applications including open-domain question answering and dialogue, is widely used in those areas and code generation, and aims to make generated text more accurate and credible. Its central challenge is that retrieval can yield fake, noisy, fragmented, incomplete, incorrect, or merely semantically related information, which may interfere with or mislead the language model. The records recast the role of LLMs in RAG as information refinement. In the described training setting, target generation is conditioned on constructed retrieved texts; the Correct and Complete task trains models to use noisy retrieved knowledge. INFO-RAG is presented as an unsupervised training method for improving use of retrieved information and robustness. Evaluation spans eleven datasets and seven tasks, including scenarios with correct answers, altered answers, or no correct answers in retrieved texts. The reported results show average improvement for all four LLaMA-2 variants, and the conclusion states advantages in ICL and robustness.

l: retrieved texts, Unsupervised Information Refinement Training of Large Language Models for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Retrieved information consists of texts used with large language models. Its quality varies: it may contain needed knowledge, be incomplete or incorrect, include fake news, or be relevant without answering a question. The records describe analyzing these conditions, including replaced or absent correct answers, and report that INFO-RAG more robustly extracts useful material, resists errors and noise, supplements it with model-parameter knowledge, and produces more concise, accurate, and complete text.

l: retrieved texts, Unsupervised Information Refinement Training of Large Language Models for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Retrieved texts are contextual passages supplied to language models in retrieval-augmented generation. Their quality varies: they can contain correct, incomplete, incorrect, noisy, misleading, semantically related, complex, or lengthy information, ranging from all knowledge needed for a question to no directly usable answer. Such noise can hinder or mislead models, which may also ignore useful material. The Information Refiner perspective seeks to transform them into concise, accurate, and complete text. In experiments, systems share the same retrieved documents: top-five ColBERTv2 Wikipedia passages for several tasks, or dataset-provided contextual passages for others.

l: Information Refiner, Unsupervised Information Refinement Training of Large Language Models for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Information Refiner is the proposed role of large language models in RAG and INFO-RAG. It combines knowledge from retrieved texts with knowledge in model parameters, even when retrieved texts are incorrect, incomplete, or unhelpful. Its central purpose is to produce positive information gain and improve RAG’s information bottleneck by generating text that is more concise, accurate, and complete than the input retrieved texts. From retrieval onward, the model robustly integrates the available texts and its parameter knowledge, then outputs a refined text rather than merely repeating the retrieved material.

l: INFO-RAG, Unsupervised Information Refinement Training of Large Language Models for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: INFO-RAG is an unsupervised, low-cost, general information-refinement training method for optimizing large language models for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Its central aim is to enable language models to refine retrieved information rather than simply use it as given. It classifies retrieved texts into three scenarios: texts that are complete, incomplete or incorrect, and relevant but answerless. For each scenario, it defines positive information gain, constructs sample pairs whose outputs improve on their inputs, and creates a corresponding unsupervised training task. Each sample is processed in only one scenario to avoid data leakage. The method unfolds through data collection, data construction, and unsupervised multi-task learning. It constructs Wikipedia-based training pairs, using prefixes and simulated retrieved texts so that large language models learn to condition target continuations on them. It then mixes the three information-refinement tasks during training. Across zero-shot evaluation on eleven datasets and seven tasks, INFO-RAG improves retrieval-augmented generation performance in short-answer, multi-hop, long-form, dialogue, language-modeling, and code-generation tasks. It improves LLaMA2 by an average of 9.39% relative points in the reported zero-shot prediction experiments, improves performance in all three scenarios, and improves SearChain in the open-retrieval setting. It also enhances in-context learning and can combine with the SOTA RAG framework for further gains. Its robustness results cover changes in the ratio and position of positive passages and in the number of retrieved passages, including incorrect, incomplete, and noisy retrieved texts. Finally, it enhances RAG while avoiding catastrophic forgetting: on MMLU without RAG, it performs close to the original LLaMA-2.

INFO-RAG improves average performance by 9.39% relative points, outperforms LLaMA-2 with RAG overall, and remains close to the original model on MMLU without RAG.

l: Scenario 1, Unsupervised Information Refinement Training of Large Language Models for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Scenario 1 is a setting where retrieved texts already contain all knowledge needed for a question and correct answers are selected using cover EM. It requires large language models to extract correct knowledge, remove irrelevant information, and produce direct, concise responses; INFO-RAG shows an advantage.

l: Scenario 2, Unsupervised Information Refinement Training of Large Language Models for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Scenario 2 concerns retrieved texts containing usable but incomplete or incorrect knowledge, created by randomly replacing correct answers with phrases of the same properties. It requires large language models to verify content using their parameter knowledge, retain accurate information, rectify errors, and complete what is missing. INFO-RAG and Correct and Complete and Contextual Stimulation show gains in this scenario.

l: Scenario 3, Unsupervised Information Refinement Training of Large Language Models for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Scenario 3 is a set of very difficult or long-tail questions whose retrieved texts contain no correct, usable answers, selected using cover EM. It is harder than Scenario 2 because retrieval models cannot find anything that solves the questions. Although the texts may be semantically related, large language models must use that context to stimulate knowledge in their parameters; INFO-RAG still shows an advantage.

l: knowledge, Unsupervised Information Refinement Training of Large Language Models for Retrieval-Augmented Generation

l: question, Unsupervised Information Refinement Training of Large Language Models for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: The question determines which type of information refinement is needed. It may be answered directly from retrieved texts, require correction or completion of those texts, or require LLMs to use semantically related context to stimulate additional knowledge.

l: unsupervised multi-task learning, Unsupervised Information Refinement Training of Large Language Models for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Unsupervised multi-task learning, introduced in INFO-RAG, constructs unlabeled training data from English Wikipedia as sentence prefixes, continuations, and retrieved contexts. It continues pre-trained large language models on three mixed tasks, using unsupervised and prefix language-modeling paradigms, and is presented as fundamentally improving retrieval-augmented generation performance and generalization across natural- and programming-language tasks.

l: Contextual Stimulation, Unsupervised Information Refinement Training of Large Language Models for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Contextual Stimulation is a Scenario 3 and INFO-RAG training task. It removes the target sentence from retrieved texts but retains semantically relevant neighboring sentences, requiring the model to generate the target continuation from context and its own knowledge. It makes up 40% of mixed-training batches, gains when trained separately, and helps produce the strongest result with Correct and Complete and Select and Copy.

l: Correct and Complete, Unsupervised Information Refinement Training of Large Language Models for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Correct and Complete is an INFO-RAG training task, used as 40% of batches in mixed training. It identifies informative tokens through word-distribution instability across model layers, masks and replaces tokens to simulate incomplete, incorrect, and correct knowledge, and trains the model to extract, correct, and complete damaged sentences from processed retrieved sets. Separate training gains improve further with Contextual Stimulation.

l: Select and Copy, Unsupervised Information Refinement Training of Large Language Models for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Select and Copy is a training task for Scenario 1 that uses English Wikipedia sentences as retrieved texts. It supplies all sentences in a set and trains the model to identify the sentence matching a prefix and copy its target continuation, addressing extraction of correct knowledge from complex texts. It forms 20% of batches because it is simple for LLMs, but alone causes overfitting and harms performance; with Correct and Complete and Contextual Stimulation, it contributes to the best result.

It supports open-domain question answering, soft filling, and language modeling, with ColBERTv2 retrieving five passages per example. Standard language-model training on it does not improve LLaMA-2, so INFO-RAG’s gains are not merely from additional training.

It aims to accurately extract correct information while avoiding interference from incorrect information. Its tasks select concise knowledge, correct or complete noisy knowledge, or use relevant context to stimulate generation; Correct and Complete and Contextual Stimulation help models learn this paradigm and improve correct-answer extraction.

l: RAG-Studio: Towards In-Domain Adaptation of Retrieval Augmented Generation Through Self-Alignment
s: This paper presents RAG-Studio, a self-aligned framework for adapting a general Retrieval-Augmented Generation system to a specialized domain using only a target-domain corpus and synthetic data. Its central goal is to make a general dense retriever and LLM generator operate as a cohesive domain-specific RAG system, addressing limited domain training data and LLMs’ difficulty using retrieved context effectively. RAG-Studio generates questions and answers from corpus passages, retrieves further contexts, and evaluates and refines examples. Using Chain-of-Thought prompting, the generator classifies passages as helpful, irrelevant, or misleading before answering. The framework curates rationale-based preference data to fine-tune the generator with ORPO, teaching it to incorporate domain knowledge and handle noisy contexts. It also derives positives and hard negatives from generator signals to fine-tune the retriever with a contrastive ranking loss, aligning retrieval with the generator’s preferences. In contrast to related work such as RAFT, which fine-tunes a generator using raw LLM-generated question-answer data in noisy contexts, RAG-Studio jointly trains both components with self-generated and self-curated data. Experiments use Llama-3-8B-Instruct and BGE for retrieval-augmented QA across Biomedical, Finance, Law, Computing, and TriviaQA/Wikipedia settings. RAG-Studio surpasses baselines on the five datasets except TriviaQA exact match, where DSF is first. Results attribute improvements to joint contrastive fine-tuning, tailored Chain-of-Thought prompting, and filtered synthetic data. Ablations find that tuning either component helps, while tuning both helps further; Chain-of-Thought notably improves ROUGE-L and GPT-4 accuracy evaluation, and retriever tuning particularly improves ranking quality. The approach also remains robust with stronger generator and retriever alternatives and is reported to outperform fine-tuning with human-annotated data. The paper concludes that RAG-Studio is an efficient, practical synthetic-data-only approach for specialized RAG adaptation, requiring no external data or models. Its limitations are that it handles only single-hop QA, conducts one optimization round, and optimizes only retriever and generator; multi-hop, multi-turn, multi-round, and broader module optimization remain open challenges. The work received support from the listed Beijing, Chinese national, Renmin University of China, Public Computing Cloud, and MOE-related entities.

l: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, RAG-Studio: Towards In-Domain Adaptation of Retrieval Augmented Generation Through Self-Alignment
s: Retrieval-Augmented Generation is a paradigm for enhancing text generation and applying large language models by integrating external knowledge through a standing-by retriever. It matters because authoritative, up-to-date information can improve generated outputs’ truthfulness and credibility, although off-the-shelf systems can underperform in specialized domains. The work moves from this motivation to domain adaptation through fine-tuning retrievers and generators in a unified system, then evaluates retrieval versus no retrieval. Retrieval substantially improves domain-specific question answering, while fine-tuning without retrieval can reduce GPT-4 accuracy.

s: Large language models serve as generators in retrieval-augmented generation systems, where integrated retrieval can provide authoritative, up-to-date information. General models may lack updated domain-specific knowledge, deep understanding, and effective context use, and can be confused by irrelevant context. They are therefore fine-tuned, including jointly with retrievers and synthetic or self-generated data, to use retrieved information more proficiently in specialized domains.

s: The retriever is a dense retriever in a unified RAG system that selects top-K passages from a domain corpus for synthetic questions, excluding the ground passage. Initially limited by general-purpose training and lacking updated domain-specific knowledge and deep understanding in specialized contexts, it is jointly fine-tuned with synthetic data and the generator. It receives training and generation signals from LLM self-feedback elicited through Chain-of-Thought prompting, aligning retrieval with LLM preferences. As a result, it brings in more precise, helpful contextual information and reduces misleading contexts for a specific domain.

s: Specialized domains, including medical, finance, law, private enterprise databases, biomedical information, and computing, challenge general RAG systems because of insufficient updated knowledge and deep understanding. RAG-Studio adapts such systems autonomously and showed superior performance across these domains in extensive experiments.

l: RAG-Studio, RAG-Studio: Towards In-Domain Adaptation of Retrieval Augmented Generation Through Self-Alignment
s: RAG-Studio is a self-aligned training framework and retrieval-augmented generation method for autonomously adapting a general RAG system to a specialized domain. Starting with a target-domain corpus, a general retriever, and a general LLM generator, it identifies useful domain knowledge, samples passages, generates synthetic question-answer pairs, and self-curates preference-training samples. It requires no external datasets or models for training. The resulting synthetic data is used to fine-tune both the generator and retriever into a cohesive in-domain RAG system; reported setups use Llama-3-8B-Instruct, BGE, 3,000 synthetic samples per dataset, and LoRA for generator fine-tuning. Across four domain-specific datasets and TriviaQA, it generally outperforms baselines, including RAFT across five datasets and DSF on reported ROUGE-L and GPT-4 accuracy comparisons; it also exceeds human-annotated fine-tuning data by 5.1% on automated metrics and 3.2% on GPT-4 evaluation scores. Its current scope is single-hop question answering, one optimization round, and only retriever and generator optimization.

s: A specialized domain corpus is a collection of passages that grounds RAG-Studio. It begins as input for identifying domain knowledge, yields passages for synthetic question-answer pairs and retrieved context, and ultimately supports training-data synthesis and adaptation of general RAG models to a specific domain.

l: domain knowledge, RAG-Studio: Towards In-Domain Adaptation of Retrieval Augmented Generation Through Self-Alignment
s: RAG-Studio identifies useful domain knowledge from a specialized domain corpus. This knowledge supports the synthesis of training data for adapting the RAG system.

l: synthetic data, RAG-Studio: Towards In-Domain Adaptation of Retrieval Augmented Generation Through Self-Alignment
s: Synthetic data is the sole training basis for RAG-Studio, produced from specialized domain-corpus passages without external datasets or models. It contains generated question-answer pairs, retrieved contextual passages, raw training samples, preference-training samples, and retriever-training signals. Generation prompts a model to create questions and answers, retrieves additional passages, and uses self-feedback to curate and refine samples for joint fine-tuning of the RAG system. Across datasets, 3,000 samples are generated per dataset. Filtering is crucial: filtered data improves RAG performance and substantially exceeds raw data, with average relative gains of 6.6% in ROUGE-L and 4.8% in accuracy, and it outperforms human-annotated data in reported fine-tuning experiments.

s: Retrieval-augmented generation is a question-answering system with a retriever and generator, including large language models. It retrieves relevant information from an external knowledge database, then generates an answer using that information. RAG-Studio adapts RAG systems to domains by jointly fine-tuning both components with synthetic domain-specific training data.

l: Optimizing LLM Based Retrieval Augmented Generation Pipelines in the Financial Domain
s: This document is a 2024 NAACL Human Language Technologies Industry Track paper, “Optimizing LLM Based Retrieval Augmented Generation Pipelines in the Financial Domain,” by Yiyun Zhao, Hanoz Bhathena, Prateek Singh, Saket Sharma, Bernardo Ramos, Aviral Joshi, and Swaroop Gadiyaram of JPMorgan Chase & Co.’s Machine Learning Center of Excellence. It studies Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) for financial question answering, aiming to ground large language model outputs in current, domain-specific material. The authors benchmark six LLMs, including GPT-4, GPT-3.5-Turbo, and Llama-2 models, over 15 retrieval conditions, nine prompts, and two banking datasets: webpages and policy guides. These datasets pair real user questions with relevant document chunks and human-labeled answer spans. The evaluation measures answer quality with token F1 and measures instruction following through structured formatting and direct quotation. Retrieval conditions vary gold-document availability, document number, ranking, and Retriever-Only versus Retriever-W-GT settings. The study first establishes that generative LLMs generally beat extractive baselines, while showing that missing relevant material, more distractors, and lower-ranked relevant documents degrade answers. Its policy-guide experiments further show that retrieving the gold document helps, but that models remain vulnerable to noise, ordering, and document count. GPT-4 performs best overall; GPT-4 and GPT-3.5-Turbo are more robust to prompt changes and more accurate at structured-output instructions than Llama-2 models. The paper concludes that RAG design should prioritize retrieval recall to avoid pseudo-helpful answers without relevant evidence, while also improving precision through re-rankers or fine-tuned retrievers. It stresses that optimization must consider document ordering, not recall alone. For smaller Llama-2 models, it recommends simple instructions. The work states compliance with the ACL Code of Ethics and says user data was anonymized.

l: large language models, Optimizing LLM Based Retrieval Augmented Generation Pipelines in the Financial Domain
s: Large language models are generation models that acquire substantial parametric world knowledge during pre-training and address questions across domains. In financial retrieval augmented generation, they are grounded with up-to-date, domain-specific knowledge, though they lack customized knowledge when adapting to applications. Six models are benchmarked across retrieval scenarios: they can outperform extractive baselines, but vary in prompting sensitivity, quality, and instruction following, and show pseudo-helpfulness when relevant gold documents are absent.

l: Retrieval Augmented Generation, Optimizing LLM Based Retrieval Augmented Generation Pipelines in the Financial Domain
s: Retrieval Augmented Generation is a prominent approach for grounding LLM generations in up-to-date, domain-specific knowledge. It connects LLMs to live or updated sources by retrieving relevant documents and supplying them with the query, conversation history, and generation instructions. It can reduce hallucinations and improve answer quality without costly, brittle domain-specific fine-tuning. Its components are systematically investigated for real-world generation quality and optimized in the financial domain.

l: RAG systems, Optimizing LLM Based Retrieval Augmented Generation Pipelines in the Financial Domain
s: RAG systems combine retrieval and generation: a retriever fetches documents likely relevant to a user query, then the documents, query, conversation history, and instructions enter an LLM context for answer generation. Their outputs are studied across six LLMs and two banking-sector datasets, evaluating answer quality, instruction following, retriever quality, document order and quantity, models, and prompts. Retrieval quality is central: when relevant context is missing or retrieval fails, systems may show pseudo-helpfulness, produce related but nonresponsive answers, and hallucinate. The analysis yields design recommendations for retrieval pipelines, prompts, and generation models.

s: GPT-4 is a frequently used LLM assessed in experiments and cited as a high-quality LLM. It is robust across prompts, resilient to prompt variations, and follows structured formatting, language-style, and structured-output instructions at high rates. Its performance declines as distractor documents increase or relevant documents rank lower, though it is less affected by noisy documents when the gold document is near the top.
